what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat certain types of cancer, including colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum) and stomach cancer (including cancer where the stomach meets the esophagus). It is typically used when other cancer treatments have not worked or are no longer working.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with food, within 1 hour after finishing your morning and evening meals. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, break, or chew them. Always wash your hands before and after handling the tablets. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your height and weight (called your body surface area). The usual schedule is to take the medicine twice a day for the first 5 days of a week, then skip 2 days, then take it again for 5 more days, then rest for the next 2 weeks. This 28-day cycle is then repeated. Never change your dose or schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at your regular time. Do not take a double dose to make up for the one you missed. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Store the tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them in their original bottle with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Caregivers who are pregnant or may become pregnant should avoid handling crushed or broken tablets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine lowers your immune system and makes it harder to fight infections. Avoid live vaccines (such as flu nasal spray, shingles, or chickenpox vaccines) while on this medicine — talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Women should not become pregnant and men should not father a child during treatment and for a period after — use reliable birth control. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you have: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; extreme tiredness or weakness; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is hard to control; blood in your stool or very dark/black stools; mouth sores that are painful or make it hard to eat or drink; shortness of breath or chest pain; yellowing of the skin or eyes; or if you think you may be pregnant. These could be signs of serious side effects that need prompt medical attention.
when_it_works: This medicine works continuously while you are taking it, but it may take several weeks or cycles before your doctor can tell if it is working for you. Your doctor will check your progress with regular blood tests and scans. Do not stop taking the medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and over): You may be more sensitive to side effects such as low blood counts, tiredness, and nausea. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments may be needed if you have moderate to severe kidney disease. This medicine has not been well studied in people with severe liver problems, so tell your doctor about any liver issues. Pregnancy: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Women of childbearing age must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant must use birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for at least 1 day after the last dose, as it may pass into breast milk and harm a nursing infant.
